title: Which primes do the sieving?
hook: Finding every prime up to 100 sounds like testing each number against every smaller one.

knows: a prime has no factors except 1 and itself
doesNotKnow: why crossing out the multiples of only 2, 3, 5 and 7 is enough up to 100

misconception: Finding all the primes up to 100 means testing each number for divisibility by every smaller number.
objective: The learner can explain that every non-prime up to 100 has a factor of at most 10, so sweeping out the multiples of 2, 3, 5 and 7 leaves exactly the 25 primes, and sweeping 11 adds nothing.

claims.text: Crossing out the multiples of 2, 3, 5 and 7 (but not the numbers themselves) from 2 to 100 leaves 25 numbers, and they are exactly the 25 primes up to 100.
claims.source: Recomputed with node, checking each survivor by trial division; the stage counts survivors from the same struck set it draws.

claims.text: Every number that is not prime is a x b with the smaller factor at most its square root, so up to 100 it has a prime factor of at most 10.
claims.source: If n = ab with a <= b then a x a <= n, so a <= sqrt(n) <= 10; any prime factor of a also divides n.

claims.text: After the sweeps of 2, 3, 5 and 7, sweeping 11 crosses out nothing new; its first multiple without a smaller factor would be 11 x 11 = 121, past 100.
claims.source: 22, 33, 44, 55, 66, 77, 88, 99 each have a factor among 2, 3, 5, 7 (checked with node).

claims.text: This crossing-out method is the sieve credited to Eratosthenes.
claims.source: Nicomachus of Gerasa, Introduction to Arithmetic I.13, attributes the sieve to Eratosthenes.

recall.question: To find every prime up to 200 by crossing out multiples, what is the largest prime you need to sweep?
recall.why: A non-prime up to 200 has a factor at most the square root of 200, about 14.1. 13 is still needed (169 = 13 x 13), but the next prime, 17, has 17 x 17 = 289, past 200.
